entries.title: Trump Says He'll Award Roger Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom
entries.summary: The pitcher had yet to receive the award after facing suspicions he used steroids during his 24-year career.
entries.content:
By Michelle L. Price and Will Weissert 

SAN ANTONIO (AP) — President Donald Trump announced Wednesday night that he would award the Presidential Medal of Freedom to fireballer Roger Clemens, calling the seven-time Cy Young winner “maybe the greatest pitcher of all time.”

Addressing a rally in San Antonio, Trump renewed his calls for Clemens to be inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame. That's an honor the pitcher known as “The Rocket” has yet to receive because of suspicions he used steroids during a 24-year career that featured time with the Boston Red Sox, Toronto Blue Jays, New York Yankees and Houston Astros.

“We’re giving him the Presidential Medal of Freedom,” Trump said. “And, along with the Congressional Medal of Honor, it’s the highest award bestowed upon anyone.”

The president continued: “He'll be in the Hall of Fame someday, but he deserves it. One of the greatest athletes, and maybe the greatest pitcher, of all time."

He added that the medal “is a big step up from the Hall of Fame.”

Trump has given the medal to various athletes during his two terms in the White House, including golfing legend Tiger Woods, former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Roger Staubach, famed Yankees closer Mariano Rivera and Lou Holtz, former coach of Notre Dame football.

He's bestowed the same honor on Elvis Presley posthumously and on Rush Limbaugh the year before the conservative radio host died.

Wednesday's surprise revelation came near the end of a Trump speech that lasted more than 100 minutes, and with the crowd having lost some of its enthusiasm. Clemens was attending the event, and the president called him to the stage, where the retired right-hander offered, “Well, I’m stunned.”

“This supersedes anything that obviously I've done in my playing career,” Clemens said. “And to get it from this man, this president, there wouldn’t be another president I’d want to get it from.”

Clemens, who was raised in Houston, said he was honored that the announcement came in Texas and added of Trump: “You’re talking about a winner. That’s a winner right there.”

Clemens, like slugger Barry Bonds and many other stars widely suspected of using performance-enhancing drugs, was repeatedly rejected by baseball writers in his bid for the Hall of Fame. There are other avenues where Clemens and others could eventually make it, but the road is not easy.

Clemens isn't the first star baseball player Trump has made a Hall of Fame case for. The president issued a posthumous federal pardon last year for the late Pete Rose, which led to Major League Baseball lifting its ban on the all-time career hits leader.

Trump has called for Rose to be inducted in the Hall of Fame too — also, so far, unsuccessfully.

entries.title: Ashley Hinson Denies Her Husband Is a ‘Shadow Lobbyist’
entries.summary: The Washington Sun previously reported that Hinson’s husband was credited with securing a meeting between insurance lobbyists and lawmakers from Iowa.
entries.content:
Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson pushed back on the suggestion by Democrat Josh Turek at the Iowa Senate debate on Wednesday that her husband is a “shadow lobbyist.”

Hinson, who is running for Senate against Turek, and her husband, Matt Arenholz, are deeply connected to the insurance industry. Past reporting by The Washington Sun revealed that Arenholz held a position at a top industry lobbying group during Hinson’s time as a member of the House of Representatives.

Turek briefly made an issue of Arenholz during the hour-long debate by saying Hinson’s husband is “operating as a shadow lobbyist.” 

“This is the corruption that we have to address,” said Turek, who tried to cast Hinson as someone who has used her time in Congress to benefit herself.

Documents previously reviewed by The Sun showed that Arenholz was credited with helping to secure a meeting for insurance lobbyists with Hinson and other lawmakers from Iowa.

A spokesperson with Hinson’s campaign told The Sun in August that the couple “maintain the highest ethical standards” and denied any untoward coordination between them. The spokesperson also said the meeting was “arranged just like any other meeting with an advocacy group.”

On Wednesday, Hinson scoffed at Turek’s characterization of her family.

“My husband's not a lobbyist. He's an insurance agent,” Hinson said at the debate. “He works in our basement. He's still working at home tonight while he's home with our kids.”

Iowa voters have not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008. But in a cycle that appears favorable to Democrats, Iowa’s Senate race has become especially competitive. The Cook Political Report labeled the seat a “toss up” in part because of the financial strain caused by the war in Iran and the Trump administration’s tariffs, which has led to backlash in the heavily agricultural state.

Hinson and Turek agreed that Iowa farmers are “hurting” and pointed to the war in Iran as the reason.

Turek, who uses a wheelchair due to his spina bifida, said his disability stems from his father’s exposure to Agent Orange while fighting in Vietnam and warned of the “generational” cost of “forever wars.”

Hinson agreed that the war in Iran should end. In private audio obtained earlier this year by Politico, Hinson acknowledged that the war had become a “political liability.”

Pressed on Wednesday about why she had previously voted against a series of House resolutions calling on President Donald Trump to halt the war, Hinson said that a “successful” end to the conflict hinges on ensuring Iran does not have nuclear capabilities and that allies in the region are safeguarded.

entries.title: Capitals Beat Penguins, 5-3, in Home Opener
entries.content:
By Noah Trister

Tom Wilson had a goal and two assists, and the Washington Capitals held on for a win in Alex Ovechkin's final home opener, 5-3 over the Pittsburgh Penguins on Wednesday night.

Anthony Beauvillier, Pierre-Luc Dubois, Alex Tuch and Ryan Leonard also scored for the Capitals, who introduced their roster one by one before the game, saving Ovechkin for last. The Russian star's two kids handled that announcement, and the crowd gave a standing ovation.

Ovechkin announced earlier in the week that this season would be the last in the NHL for the league's career leader in goals.

Bryan Rust, Tommy Novak and Nick Robertson scored for the Penguins, who nearly rallied from a 4-1 second-period deficit.

This is the 22nd straight season Ovechkin and Pittsburgh's Sidney Crosby have played against each other at some point. Only one forward duo in NHL history has clashed in more consecutive seasons: Mark Messier and Ron Francis, who played each other in 23.

Crosby was on the ice for every Washington even-strength goal, finishing with a minus-4. His only career minus-5 was March 6, 2014, at San Jose.

Beauvillier opened the scoring for Washington after just 23 seconds. The Penguins needed less than a minute to tie it on Bryan Rust's goal from in close.

Veteran defenseman Kris Letang of the Penguins played a blind pass in his own zone and paid for it when the puck went to Pierre-Luc Dubois behind the net. One pass later, and Wilson was making it 2-1 Capitals from alone in front.

Those same two players combined in the second period to make it 3-1 after another Pittsburgh mistake. Silovs went behind his net, but when he played the puck along the boards Wilson was right there to collect it and find Dubois in front.

Tuch intercepted a pass at his own blue line, and suddenly he and Wilson were bearing down alone on Silovs. After two quick passes back and forth, Tuch scored to put Washington up by three.

Novak quickly answered for the Penguins, and then Robertson cut the lead to one with a deflection from the slot.

It was 4-3 after two, but Leonard's power-play goal in the third gave the Capitals a bit of a cushion.

Later in the third, Washington goalie Logan Thompson kept the lead at two by stopping Blake Lizotte on a breakaway just after the Pittsburgh forward came out of the penalty box.

Declan Carlile of the Penguins was shaken up in the third after Dubois was assessed a minor penalty for boarding him.

entries.title: Election Deniers Have Trump's Ear on a Voting Machine Conspiracy
entries.summary: Conspiracy theorist Tina Peters and other allies want to convince the White House it already has the authority to probe voting systems.
entries.content:
Election deniers peddling conspiracies about voting machines have gotten President Donald Trump’s attention less than a month before the midterms.

Trump on Monday reportedly met with conspiracy theorist Tina Peters, who for months has been urging Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to investigate voting machines using power purportedly vested to him under the executive order, which declared a national emergency on certain Chinese software and parts.

“The president is taking it seriously,” former U.S. Pardon Attorney Ed Martin said Tuesday on an episode of the conservative talk show “Real America’s Voice.”

Martin also invoked Trump’s priority elections legislation, which has been stalled in the Senate for months, as a reason to focus on a voting machine crackdown.

“If the Congress won’t pass the SAVE America Act — and they won’t — then the president’s going to have to do what he’s going to do,” Martin said. “It’s not a local issue when it’s national security. And it’s clearly national security.”

The push to use an EO signed during Trump’s first term comes as Republicans in the administration rush to implement efforts to combat unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud. As the Nov. 3 midterms draw closer, longtime right-wing concerns about voting machines — which the government has already approved for states to use on Election Day — have increasingly circulated among fringe conspiracy circles and members of the Cabinet.

Central to the allegations is Peters, a former county election clerk from Colorado who was convicted in 2024 of tampering with county voting equipment before Democratic Gov. Jared Polis commuted her sentence in May. Other proponents include Martin, who left the Justice Department in August, and Republican lawyer Cleta Mitchell, who says she wants Lutnick to “announce and implement a plan” to ensure the electronic voting systems are not “compromised or manipulated.”

In recent months, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has sent a series of public letters alleging China and Russia have compromised state-owned voting machines, after a White House task force in July asserted that China had obtained extensive American voter-registration data. Because nearly all U.S. voting machines contain parts made in China, DHS asserts, using those systems would allow foreign adversaries to sway election results.

Experts from the Brennan Center for Justice and other nonpartisan democracy researchers note that while all voting systems possess inherent technological vulnerabilities, certified machines used in U.S. elections remain fundamentally secure and reliable, with no evidence of widespread manipulation.

In September, Mullin announced his plan to help states transition from electronic voting to paper ballots, carry out audits of voting equipment and push out software updates before November.

The federal government lacks the power to more directly intervene in locally administered elections: Under Mullin’s proposal, state participation in those security initiatives would be voluntary.

But Peters wants to go further. Her plan, detailed on her website, puts Lutnick at the center of a more aggressive effort to require states to abandon the use of vote-counting machines in favor of hand-tallied ballots.

The push to enlist the commerce secretary dates at least to August 2025. Emails obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight last month show that White House chief of staff Susie Wiles connected election-denial activists Will Huff and Conrad Reynolds with Martin through a staffer, partially in hopes of getting Peters a meeting with Trump, who had aggressively lobbied Polis for her commutation.

In email correspondence between Martin, Huff and Reynolds, the three discussed lobbying the administration to use the 2019 executive order to order Lutnick to seize voting equipment.

Huff said the move “can immediately force states to move to hand-marked and hand-counted ballots like the President wishes.” The proposals also included eliminating most mail and absentee voting and sharply curtailing early voting.

In an August episode of their podcast, Reynolds said Lutnick gave the pair “two-and-a-half hours of his time” to hear their proposal. He said the secretary said he was “shocked at what we had to say” and “would be getting on it.”

Commerce’s involvement in the administration’s election integrity agenda has never been a public-facing strategy. The department did not respond to multiple requests for comment about Lutnick's involvement.

When asked about Peters’ visit with Trump at the Oval Office, a DHS spokesperson said that “concerns over voting processes, data security and registration practices have made it clear that action is required” and pointed The Washington Sun to its election infrastructure plan issued last month. 

A Department of Justice spokesperson told The Sun the department isn’t involved in any plans to sow doubt about voting systems.

“The Department of Justice does not support, and is making no preparations to support, efforts to declare certified voting equipment unreliable or unusable absent credible, verified evidence and the legal process for doing so. Any suggestion that such an initiative is underway at the Department is false,” the spokesperson said.

The White House refused to confirm the content of Trump’s meeting with Peters and declined to give additional comment.

The 2019 order championed by Peters and Martin initially was mandated by Trump to declare a national emergency on any critical infrastructure, which includes election systems built using materials or software produced in China. It grants the commerce secretary the power to “prohibit any transaction” of American infrastructure supplied by foreign adversaries.

Martin said Peters brought her plan to Trump earlier this week. The two discussed having Lutnick potentially mandate a federal investigation of state-owned election technology for connections to Chinese parts, which could empower him to order mandatory restrictions or changes to voting machines ahead of the midterms.

“Time is now the controlling variable. The U.S. does not need to prove a foreign adversary already changed a past election result before acting,” Peters’ website states.

Elections experts say hand-counting votes can be slow or introduce errors, while Democrats say manual counts set up additional opportunities to sow doubt about election integrity.

Last month, Senate Democrats accused DHS of trying to federalize elections through pressure campaigns concerning access to voter data and grant funding — characterizing the administration’s recent actions as “calculated efforts to undermine confidence in our elections.”

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Tuesday that his party has been preparing “for months to stop unconstitutional, corrupt schemes” like what Peters proposes.

“We’re taking nothing for granted,” Schumer wrote on X. “And we’ll be ready to see and beat these ghouls in court.”

entries.title: Everything Is Bigger in Texas — Including the Number of Protests at Trump’s Rally
entries.summary: About a dozen people were escorted from the venue as the president was interrupted multiple times at a San Antonio campaign event
entries.content:
President Donald Trump’s rally in San Antonio for Senate candidate Ken Paxton and other Republicans was interrupted multiple times within minutes of him taking the stage Wednesday, as protesters shouted from the floor of the Freeman Coliseum.

One took a video of himself as he walked toward the exit, only to be rushed from behind by an elderly man in a red Make America Great Again hat, who appeared to yank the protester’s shirt and hair before other attendees pulled him away.

“These are paid protesters. They're paid by enemies of our nation,” Trump said after another protester interruption minutes later.

“If there are any more paid protesters, please raise your hand and get the hell out of here,” the president added.

One protester exited while being insulted by Trump about his weight. Two more were removed while the crowd chanted, “U-S-A!” Several protesters, including one wearing the Spanish National Team’s World Cup kit who yelled in the direction of the stage, were marched out by police.
Trump (3545x2363, AR: 1.50)About a dozen people disrupted the rally before leaving voluntarily or being forcibly removed from the arena during Trump’s speech, according to the reporters traveling with the president.

The disruptions caused Trump to pause several times as the crowd yelled to drown out the protesters’ chants. As the interruptions continued, Trump temporarily turned from mocking Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico to making fun of the protesters trying to steal the spotlight — starting with a “mom” joke.

“He’s going back home to mom,” Trump said as the first protester, a young man, walked away from the stage. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”

Shortly after, Trump returned to Talarico, and to one of his favorite attacks on the Democrat — calling him a vegan, and reducing the Texas Senate race to a voter’s preference for a prime cut of steak or a plate of tofu.

“He’s been forced to eat meat for political reasons, and he’s throwing up all over the place,” Trump said. The president claimed Talarico would swallow a few ribs and then spit them out behind a tent. He compared the alleged diet to Paxton’s.

“I have a feeling Ken likes meat,” Trump said of the Texas attorney general.

Talarico has repeatedly said he isn’t a vegan, and PolitiFact rated Paxton’s claim about Talarico as false in May when he first levied it. Talarico’s campaign responded at the time with a photograph of the Democratic nominee eating barbecue in a Texas flag shirt.

Trump also announced that he will give the Presidential Medal of Freedom to former Major League pitcher Roger Clemens. Clemens won seven Cy Young Awards but was left out of the Hall of Fame after allegations of steroid use.

The president called the medal a “big step up” from being enshrined among the legends of America’s pastime.

The rally was Trump’s third Texas stop in under a month and part of a monthlong campaign tour ahead of Election Day. His appearance alongside Paxton followed a series of leaks from the attorney general’s private conversations. On Wednesday, Axios reported that Paxton blamed his campaign troubles on issues that he couldn’t control, namely the cost of fuel and the Iran war.

Paxton also blamed the GOP midterm convention for his sinking poll numbers. A New York Times and Siena University poll released Oct. 4 found Talarico ahead 51% to 45%. In the survey, voters also said they believe Talarico would do a better job handling many issues on which the race has centered: cost of living, health care and tariffs.

On Wednesday, Trump was asked in the Oval Office if he regretted endorsing Paxton because of the leaked comments. Trump defended Paxton, saying that he would “be a great senator.”

“And no, I would have no regrets at all,” the president added.

entries.title: Judge Blocks an ‘Arbitrary’ Trump Policy That Bars Detainees From a Crucial Visa Screening Step
entries.summary: Many detained immigrants were trapped in a policy loophole that prevented them from achieving legal status.
entries.content:
A federal judge in Washington blocked a Trump administration policy that prevented detained immigrants from completing the fingerprint screenings required to apply for legal status.

In his ruling Wednesday, Judge Amir H. Ali called the December policy “arbitrary and capricious” and ordered the government to resume collecting biometric information from detainees with pending applications while the lawsuit proceeds.

Amir said that the government, without any explanation, “effectively denies immigration relief to a whole category of people irrespective of their eligibility for the status they have applied for.”

A group of detained immigrants filed the class-action lawsuit against the Trump administration in April, claiming the Department of Homeland Security intentionally blocked them from legal status by denying them the required screenings. Some of the plaintiffs involved had already been held in detention centers for over a year, and many are proven survivors of “child abuse, domestic violence and human trafficking,” the ruling says.

The group’s claim that the policy was unlawful is likely valid, Ali wrote, because Justice Department officials had not offered a “rational explanation” for implementing new biometrics rules.

The administration said the policy deters the filing of “frivolous claims and provides operational consistency.” But the court agreed with the plaintiffs that the rule largely blocked legitimate applicants, adding that collecting biometrics helps officials verify identities and conduct background checks.

When the judge asked government lawyers during a hearing how the policy served its stated goals, an attorney responded: “That’s a good question. I don’t have an answer to that right now,” the ruling states.

Ali’s order suspends the policy for any detained immigrants with pending U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services applications — rejecting the administration’s argument that relief should apply only to those named in the initial legal complaint.

The ruling does not grant anyone a visa or resolve the case. Ali declined to issue a separate preliminary injunction to that end, finding that suspension of the policy was sufficient for now.

The administration must report back to the court concerning compliance with the injunction by Oct. 21.

entries.title: Talk to Tom: Michelin Stars, Anniversary Recs and D.C.’s Best Thai
entries.summary: Plus: How to eat like a restaurant critic.
entries.content:
Welcome to Talk to Tom, the dining-advice column that aims to point you toward good meals, steer you from the dross and solve your pressing restaurant queries. Look for a fresh Q&A every Thursday in this space.

Questions and comments can be submitted to TalkToTom@washingtonsun.com. Submissions may be edited for length and clarity.

We are coming up on 10 years of D.C. receiving its first Michelin stars.  What do you think of the award? 

Hey, if I were a chef, I might aspire to recognition from the French guide, too. It’s the most famous culinary award someone can receive, and the guide’s been around since 1900.

My short answer to your timely question: The Michelin guide is best used in France, where it originated. I’ve not had similar luck with the publication in other European countries, or in the U.S., for that matter.

It got off to a bumpy start in D.C. when it rolled out in October 2016. A decade ago, I was critical of its many blind spots, including the omission of such first-rate restaurants as the late (Greek) Komi and the modern Indian Rasika. Last year, Michelin demoted the Inn at Little Washington from three stars, its highest rating, to two stars. Yet the Virginia dining destination has never been better. (I say that having eaten there almost 30 times.)

There’s a lot of mystery surrounding Michelin’s anonymous inspectors. I tend to place my trust in local reviewers vetted by their publications. Whether you agree with them or not, at least you can view their body of work and bios online. My respected peers in the industry tend to visit restaurants multiple times and have sufficient budgets to support the effort. That’s not necessarily the case with Michelin, which has created in some American markets a pay-for-play situation. See: Denver and Orlando, among other cities whose tourism organizations contributed financial support to the guide.

In the U.S. and abroad, I’ve been to plenty of Michelin-ranked restaurants. I’ve found the guides’ one-star establishments appeal to me most, while some of the “more stars” tend to feel the same, regardless of where they are in the world, probably because they’re chasing Michelin standards.

Bottom line: At the end of the day, Michelin is a tire factory doling out stars (or not). I realize we’re all plants that need a little H20 — and awards are nice — but chefs should understand there’s plenty of honor and value in cooking to please the general public.

There are a million Thai places in D.C. Do you have a favorite?

Let me preface my answer by sharing that the original Donsak Thai in Woodley Park is so close to my home that I can walk there in two minutes. So that’s where I tend to go when I’m in the mood for, say, chicken meatball skewers, shrimp dumplings, bamboo shoot salad, and green curry, among other prizes.

Elsewhere in the city, I love a seat at the bar at Baan Mae in Shaw, where monkey characters on the wall and parasols on the ceiling make a fanciful backdrop to the cooking of chef Seng Luangrath, who also owns the excellent Padaek dining rooms in Arlington and Falls Church. Her summer rolls alone add up to a party.

I haven’t eaten at them recently, but the attractive Baan Siam in Mount Vernon Triangle and Soi 38 downtown have both offered memorable meals in recent years.

I’d love to hear which Thai restaurants you and other readers frequent. Send me your picks, please.

How do you do this job without gaining a ton of weight? 

One of the first things I did when I became food critic of The Washington Post in 2000 was hire a trainer, which might sound like a yuppie affectation until you consider that the job involves constant eating out, and no matter how careful you are, a steady stream of fried food, rich sauces, cocktails, meat, bread (gotta sample the bread baskets!) and desserts add up. I viewed exercise as insurance. Plus, you just feel better, mentally and physically, when you move more than your utensils from hand to mouth.

Here at The Washington Sun, I’m still eating out as often as five or six meals a week. So at home, I eat pretty clean — fresh fruit and cottage cheese for breakfast is a near-daily habit. In restaurants, I rarely finish a dish, preferring to let others at the table do that or take home leftovers. (I hate wasting food, but I don’t necessarily want it in my fridge.) At this point, for instance, I can judge a steak in about three bites. And if it’s just two of us, I’ll order wine by the glass versus a bottle. Alice Waters of Chez Panisse fame once shared that her simple trick for losing weight was cutting out alcohol.

Restraint sounds boring, but that’s my mantra — unless, of course, I’m in front of a plate of french fries at Et Voila! in the Palisades or a tavern-style pizza at La Merna in Dupont Circle. “Moderation in moderation” is another rule I follow.

Can you give me a recommendation for a wedding anniversary dinner under $200 total?

You don’t say how many years you’re celebrating, where you live, what your food preferences are, or whether you drink (the more details, the better I can assist), so I’m going to throw out a few different scenarios and hope one fits.

In the District, I’m a big fan of the L’Ardente and the whimsical Italian script from chef David Deshaies. His open kitchen is the source of such extreme pleasures as a lemony, goat cheese-filled ravioli and (sharable) flaming tiramisu, priced at $24 and $20 respectively, everything served beneath wooden beams and Murano glass chandeliers.

On the more relaxed, but still excellent, side, there’s the walk-in Bar Del Monte in Mount Pleasant, where I generally fill up on appetizers washed back with something from owner Oliver Pastan’s thoughtful wine list. The Italian-leaning small plates — grilled lamb skewers, a fritto misto whose batter any Japanese tempura master would envy — range from $17 to $24, “with tip included,” Pastan says, referencing the fact the gratuity is built into the cost of the food. (Sweet. No math for me!)

In Northern Virginia, I’d head to the always-hospitable Ada’s on the River in Alexandria, the neighborly Maple Room in Vienna, or the convivial Mama Chang in Fairfax. In closer-in Maryland, I’d gravitate to Melina for good Greek in a stylish environment in North Bethesda and Lime & Cilantro in Silver Spring, where chef Danny Chavez slips lots of “wow” moments into his modern Latin cooking. I love his takes on hummus (made with corn), short ribs (ennobled with mole), and his mom’s tamales, which he once took off the menu to so much protest that he brought them back in a matter of weeks. Now? “They aren’t going anywhere,” says the El Salvador native.

What is an unfilled spot in the D.C. restaurant scene? What do you wish we had here?

First, allow me to address some holes that have been filled in the city. Among the welcome changes since I became a stomach for hire are the rise of a bunch of new restaurant zones — Shaw, Union Market, and the Navy Yard come to mind — and what a lot of us call “neighborhood” spots, meaning places where you can go once a week or so when you want a break from your own kitchen but don’t want to go the carryout route. I’m thinking of venues where you can sit down at a table and enjoy a nice roast chicken, plate of pasta, some curry, dumplings or steak frites and the check won’t resemble anything close to your monthly condo fee.

Now to your question: The District could use more Nordic representation, better regional Chinese, and a serious delicatessen along the lines of what the Big Apple offers. Oh, and more (and more refined) desserts. I can practically count the city’s top pastry chefs on one hand, a problem the pandemic only made worse. When push comes to shove, most restaurants are going to hire a dishwasher or a line cook instead of a dedicated sweets maker. Which is why we see a sea of creme brûlée, tiramisu and (yawn) sorbets on menus.

entries.title: Schumer's Leadership Chances Are Looking Better Than Ever
entries.summary: Despite a rocky tenure as Democratic leader, Schumer doesn’t face a challenge, but most Senate Democrats don’t want to talk about his political future yet.
entries.content:
It wasn’t long ago that Chuck Schumer was the most vilified man in the Democratic Party, but his political fortunes have boomeranged, and he appears on track to become the elected Senate leader again, barring a massive Democratic underperformance.

Last fall, the New York senator faced intense backlash from angry Democrats who felt he wasn’t doing enough to stand up to Donald Trump as leader of the opposition in the Senate. Many wanted him to step aside and make way for someone new.

Now, with most polls pointing to a blue wave in the November midterm elections, Democrats are on the verge of something many believed near impossible: a majority in the upper chamber next year, thanks in part to Schumer’s strong fundraising efforts and successful recruitment of quality candidates in battleground states like North Carolina, Ohio and Alaska.

Schumer isn’t issuing any “I told you so’s” to his critics, at least not yet. But he’s feeling good about where things stand right now. Trump’s poll numbers have cratered amid a national affordability crisis and the ongoing war in Iran. Panicked Republicans are pulling resources from battleground states in order to defend seats in red states.

“I have focused totally, like the North Star, on winning back the Senate, and I think people recognize that we have had a lot of success and we're getting very close,” Schumer told The Washington Sun last week.

Schumer is planning to run for another term as leader in November, regardless of whether Democrats win the Senate or not. But it’s not clear anyone would challenge him for the job even if they lose.

High-profile progressives who have called for new leadership in the Democratic Party in the past — senators like Cory Booker of New Jersey, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Chris Murphy of Connecticut, and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan — seem to be focused more on the national stage and laying the groundwork for possible campaigns for the White House in 2028.

Dick Durbin, the No. 2 Senate Democrat, is retiring this year, and Hawaii Sen. Brian Schatz is in line to replace him as party whip. Amy Klobuchar, the No. 3 Senate Democrat and another member of Schumer’s leadership team, is leaving the Senate, favored to win her bid to become governor of Minnesota. Sens. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts seem more interested in influencing the direction of the party from the outside and are not viewed as likely leadership candidates.

Democratic senators aren’t sure whether anyone else would even run for Schumer’s job.

“Generally, this is a pretty conflict-averse group of people,” said a Democratic senator who requested anonymity to speak freely about Schumer’s future. “Is there somebody in the caucus who would step up? If there is, I'm not sure who it is.”

The senator warned that could change if Democrats underperform in the November elections and whether Schumer ultimately decides to seek another term in 2028.

“Does he ask [the caucus] whether he wants to stay for two years, and is he going to run for reelection? What does that look like?” the lawmaker said. “There's been lots of different ways that leaders have transitioned out of leadership. Would he do what [former House Speaker Nancy] Pelosi did, or what [former Senate Majority Leader Mitch] McConnell did?”

“Who the fuck knows? I mean, I think it's totally in flux,” the senator added.

Democrats have sought to distance themselves from Schumer on the campaign trail, especially after last year’s government funding fights, when the party failed to get major concessions from the White House. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, Troy Jackson in Maine, Juliana Stratton in Illinois and Adam Hamilton in Kansas have all said they would not vote for Schumer as leader.

Scott Colom, Mississippi’s Democratic Senate candidate, has similarly called for change, arguing it’s “a big problem” that both Democratic leaders in Congress — Schumer and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries — hail from Brooklyn, New York.

“That's not a good thing for a national party to have two people who live within that close proximity. For me, I would really prefer somebody that understood rural America,” Colom told The Sun in a recent interview.
Chuck Schumer Hakeem Jeffries (4500x2999, AR: 1.50)Other Democratic Senate candidates like former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown and former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper have not explicitly committed to supporting Schumer, but they haven’t ruled it out, either. Schumer’s political operation has invested large sums of money to support their campaigns, as well as the campaigns of other critics.

But leader elections for both the Senate majority and minority take place in a secret ballot vote that’s expected to happen soon after the November elections. The public won’t know if Schumer’s critics followed through with voting for someone else.

Democratic senators have been loath to discuss the sensitive topic of Schumer and their caucus leadership in public. Most are taking a wait-and-see approach depending on the results of midterms.

“That’s putting the cart before the horse. I’m just trying to win the election,” Van Hollen said, adding that he’s currently focused on campaigning for Democrats across the country.

Some progressives have floated the idea of Van Hollen as leader, but the Maryland Democrat told The Sun earlier this year that he’s considering a presidential bid instead. Operating from within the halls of Congress, he reflected, is “not a successful recipe for actually getting change.” Still, he hasn’t totally ruled it out.
Chuck Schumer, Cory Booker (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)Booker, another likely 2028 contender, also punted when asked about the subject this week.

“I'm focused right now on winning, and then I think we need to have a family conversation about whether people are getting gavels and leading committees or who's going to be the leader of the Senate,” he told CNN.

Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona, who is also weighing a 2028 run, said he expected Schumer to remain as leader if Democrats win or lose the Senate, while Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey said he wanted assurances that his bill to provide free, comprehensive health care for every child and young adult in America up to age 26 will be a priority before making a decision on leadership.

“I hope to be able to have leadership and partners in the Senate that want to help me push these types of ideas forward,” Kim said. “This is not meant to be a messaging bill. It's something I actually want to get done.”

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island) credited Schumer's "stellar candidate recruitment" for putting Democrats in a "very strong position to take back the Senate."

"Republicans spending big to save Senate seats in red states would have been unthinkable this time last year," Whitehouse added in his statement.

Progressive activists also want Senate Democratic leadership to embrace more ambitious policies like Medicare for All in the next Congress, which wouldn’t have a chance of passing while Trump is president, but it could help the party set the terms of debate ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

But most of all, they want a change at the top.

“The leader should be concerned,” said Joseph Geevarghese, the executive director of Our Revolution, the progressive group founded by Sanders in 2016. “There is a shift in the base of the Democratic Party, and the grassroots want leaders who will fight aggressively against the Trump administration and their overreach.”

Schumer, at least, is ignoring the haters as Democrats strive to flip at least four seats needed to win the majority.

“Our caucus is totally unified,” he said at a press conference last week. “We're in great shape. Everyone is really very, very pleased with where we are today compared to where we were 20 months ago under our leadership, and we're fighting hard. We're on the edge of taking back the Senate.”

entries.title: Why Republicans’ Top Recruit Is Struggling in Purple New Hampshire
entries.summary: Some experts thought John E. Sununu could buck national headwinds, but it’s easier said than done.
entries.content:
Republicans thought they had one of their best shots at flipping a Democratic Senate seat in purple New Hampshire this year after longtime Sen. Jeanne Shaheen announced her retirement. It’s looking less that way every week.

Party leaders did have reason to be hopeful, even in a difficult national environment for Republicans.

They felt they had momentum after nominating John E. Sununu in September. The former senator belongs to one of the state’s most prominent political dynasties, he has a record of distancing himself from an increasingly unpopular President Donald Trump and Republicans have millions of dollars to spend in the small state.

Many of them also thought Sununu could catch a draft from the reelection campaign of popular Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte.

But a lot of those hopes are not materializing, and not just because of a bad national political climate.

New Hampshire has a way of defying what the experts back in Washington expect, said Matthew Bartlett, a Republican strategist from the state.

“Historically, the past 10 years, we have been Republican at home and Democrats in D.C.,” Bartlett told The Washington Sun. “We are a middle finger in New England. We really have our own brand of conservatism, of this independent, maybe even libertarian streak to us.”

In fact, despite GOP optimism, Sununu has largely trailed the Democratic nominee, Rep. Chris Pappas, in recent polls. The Cook Political Report moved the race from a “toss up” to “lean Democrat” earlier this week.

Bartlett pointed to some of the reasons. For one, New Hampshire voters have a tradition of splitting the ticket, and the premise Ayotte will have coattails is probably false. In New Hampshire, the governor is on the ballot every two years, Bartlett said, meaning she has less of an impact on turnout than in a state like Pennsylvania, for example, where the governor is only on the ballot every four years.

“New Hampshire voters have never been afraid to bounce back and forth,” Bartlett said. “It ping-pongs back and forth between federal and state on the New Hampshire ballot, and I think voters are going to follow the ping-pong ball pretty consistently.”

Those unique local dynamics are compounded by the difficult national environment for Republicans across the country with rising prices linked to the war in Iran, as well as Canadian tariffs that have special relevance in the northern border state, said Dante Scala, a political science professor at the University of New Hampshire.

Pappas has centered the rising cost of living in his campaign spiel and repeatedly tried to link Sununu to the unpopular president. An AARP survey conducted in late September found that half of the voters in New Hampshire cite affordability as the top issue “driving their voting decisions this November.”

Rachel Petri, Pappas’ campaign manager, stuck to that theme in a statement to The Sun. “Chris Pappas is fighting to lower costs, end Trump’s war in Iran and tariff taxes, and stand up to a reckless Trump administration,” she said. “John Sununu is running to boost the bottom line of his corporate special interest backers.”

Sununu’s campaign did not respond to several requests for comment, but he told a local TV station that “it doesn’t make sense” to engage in a trade war with Canada and has repeatedly said he opposes the war in Iran, highlighting differences with Trump.

In an August candidate forum, Sununu said it was a “mistake” for the U.S. to enter Iran and argued that Congress should vote to reclaim its war powers after a series of failed votes to curb the administration’s military actions.

“What he’s been trying to do in his messaging is he’s trying to take full advantage of the fact that he’s been out of politics for so long and present himself as an outsider,” Scala said. “He’s leaning into presenting himself as an independent for New Hampshire ... he kind of downplays the party label and emphasizes the independent.”

Still, Scala said those differences might not be enough to overcome Democratic “enthusiasm in 2026.” Democrats saw significantly higher voter turnout than Republicans in the state’s September primary.

“The Democratic base is fired up,” Scala said. “So the Sununu name carries weight, I’m not denying that, but is it enough to overcome all of these other factors? I’m not seeing that and it’s four weeks out.”

Republicans do still have one element in their favor — the money.

Scott Spradling, a former political journalist in New Hampshire, said Republicans hold a significant spending advantage over Democrats in New Hampshire, which could be decisive in such a tight race.

The state has been flooded with mailers and television advertisements targeted at Pappas, Spradling said. And in a race this narrow and in a state with such a sparse population, how effectively both sides can leverage their campaign spending to pull over split-ticket voters could be the decisive factor.

The biggest outstanding question, though, is how far an onslaught of political spending can move the needle in the remaining month until the election.

“The Senate race is a single-digit race. Nobody’s going to debate that,” Spradling said. “It’s close enough that an investment of that much money could drive up just a few more negative points for Pappas and pull out a few more Republicans to vote in this race … it all remains to be seen.”

entries.title: The White House Has Unleashed Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
entries.summary: The Trump administration now views the health secretary as more of an asset than a liability in the midterms.
entries.content:
Consider Robert F. Kennedy Jr. unleashed.

Muzzled earlier this year by White House officials uneasy with the health secretary’s fringier views, the Trump administration is now trying to leverage Kennedy and his Make America Healthy Again movement for Republicans ahead of the midterm elections.

“They’ve given him flexibility to be himself and do his Bobby Kennedy thing,” one senior administration official told The Washington Sun.

Earlier this year, rumors flew inside and outside the administration that Kennedy would be ousted after the midterms. Mehmet Oz, the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, was seen as a possible successor, according to multiple political and career staffers.

Instead, control over Kennedy’s messaging has loosened in recent months as part of a concerted effort to put the health secretary out front, which sources in the administration say is being driven by President Donald Trump himself.

The relationship between Trump and Kennedy is “very strong,” a second administration official familiar with their relationship said. “Bobby doesn’t push super hard on it, but they have a very strong relationship.”

Better known and better liked by American voters than other members of Trump’s Cabinet, Kennedy is being deployed to election hot spots more than others in Trump’s orbit. He has visited Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, Iowa, Colorado, Texas and other states where Republicans are clinging to House and Senate seats.

Trump is cheering Kennedy’s unorthodox views. The president has urged quick results from Kennedy’s probe into autism and vaccines. Kennedy has been given license on new initiatives to address vaccine injuries. Neither Trump nor his aides pushed back publicly when Kennedy promised an anti-vaccine group last month that the administration would investigate electromagnetic fields and chemtrails.

“You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” Kennedy told the group last month.

Perhaps most tellingly, the president effectively rubber-stamped Kennedy’s efforts to change the childhood vaccine schedule with an executive order in August.

“I think Trump sent a message” with that executive order, said Del Bigtree, who served as communications director for Kennedy in his 2024 presidential campaign and runs the anti-vaccine group Informed Consent Action Network. “I think it was a huge move in imbuing confidence in Bobby that he could push forward with the work he’s trying to do.”
Trump (6901x4600, AR: 1.50)Trump’s recent moves bode well for Kennedy’s future in his administration after an initial turbulent period where Kennedy struggled to put out fires and started some of his own. In his first year, his tampering with vaccine policy inflamed tensions at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, whose director was fired after just a month, prompting the resignation of other top CDC officials.

It also marks a shift in the Trump administration’s political calculations regarding Kennedy and the MAHA movement from that of a possible liability to a possible asset.

Earlier this year, influential White House aides tightened their hold on Kennedy’s messaging, pressuring him to stay away from vaccine statements and instead focus on unprocessed foods and exercise. The administration elevated former Medicare director Chris Klomp to chief counselor of the Department of Health and Human Services in an effort to stabilize things.

The White House didn’t want Kennedy to draw in bad press. It killed a digital and TV ad campaign for his much advertised “Take Back Your Health” initiative, nervous it would generate negative attention in light of former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem’s scandals. But quietly and behind the scenes, Kennedy’s allies inside HHS continued their efforts to investigate vaccines.

There was good reason to be concerned: Majorities of Americans said they disapproved of how Kennedy was handling his job, particularly disapproving of the administration’s approach to vaccine policy, according to a KFF poll conducted in January.

Republicans did commend Kennedy for broadening their coalition in 2024 to include a coveted group of swing voters that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic: mothers who grew disillusioned with the medical establishment.

“What was frankly a brilliant strategy to gain women voters has turned into a nightmare coalition for [Democrats],” said Democratic pollster Celinda Lake.

Kennedy’s tirades against food additives and pesticides resonate with voters in both parties. And he’s slightly less disliked than other national GOP politicians. In a recent Harvard-Harris poll, 43% of voters viewed him favorably, compared to 41% for Trump and Vice President JD Vance and 38% for Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Republicans still aren’t overly eager to talk about Kennedy, whose propensity for conspiracy theories leaves some squeamish. His changes to vaccine recommendations and appointment of vaccine-skeptical researchers has frustrated some Republicans, although most have held their fire.

Five House candidates and two gubernatorial candidates whose districts and states Kennedy visited this year did not respond to an interview request from The Sun. One declined. But Rep. Tom Barrett, a Republican who hosted Kennedy in his toss-up Michigan district in June, told The Sun that the Republican Party is “better off” with Kennedy’s base in its coalition.

“He represents a brand of politics and a constituency that is outside the normal coalition,” Barrett said.

Rep. Richard Hudson, the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, declined an interview about Kennedy. In a statement provided by his spokesperson to The Sun, he said, “Secretary Kennedy connects with independents and former Democrats in a way few people in politics can.”
Election 2026 Republicans (5648x3765, AR: 1.50)Trump understood Kennedy’s value earlier this year. “I read an article today where they think Bobby is going to be really great for the Republican Party in the midterms,” the president said during a January Cabinet meeting. “I have to be very careful that Bobby likes us.”

MAHA moms know their power this November, said Zen Honeycutt, founder of the group Moms Across America.

“We are adamant about keeping [Kennedy] in office,” Honeycutt said.

If the White House plans on ousting Kennedy next year, it’s not letting on.

“Make America Healthy Again was not just a campaign slogan — it was President Trump’s pledge to tackle America’s chronic disease epidemic,” said White House spokesperson Allison Schuster. “Secretary Kennedy is rightfully going to tout these victories for the American people and keep delivering more of them in the coming weeks and months.”

James Blair, who is running Trump’s political operation this year, turned to Kennedy in July to pressure a Libertarian candidate to drop out of a competitive House race because Blair heard they respected him, The Washington Post reported.

For Republicans, Kennedy’s value also lies in his unique ability to argue that Democrats have changed. A former Democrat who began building his public profile as an environmentalist before leading an anti-vaccine group, he spent much of his 25-minute speech at the Republican midterm convention excoriating Democrats for turning into the party of “Big Pharma, Big Tech, Big Ag, Big Food, Big Insurance.”

“I realized many of the foundational values of the Democratic Party had found a new home, and it was the Republican Party,” he said, to cheers.

That type of message helps legitimize Republicans as a party that isn’t just the old GOP but one with a new influence and energy, said Charles Eisenstein, who advised Kennedy’s 2024 campaign.

“And just because he's a Kennedy — that's in and of itself legitimizing,” Eisenstein added.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: No Spa Day
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Oct. 8, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: A fated D.C. spa complex, Trayon’s latest push for acquittal and how Tom Sietsema stays trim.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 9/10. Basically as awesome as yesterday, but a bit warmer and breezier.Full forecast from Capital Weather.


THE LATEST

Relax, D.C. Or not.

An effort to bring a massive spa complex to the banks of the Anacostia River seems to have lost steam, after Ward 4 council member Janeese Lewis George — who is also likely to be D.C.’s next mayor — said she opposes it.

“I have concerns regarding the proposed development project at Poplar Point, which is one of the East Coast's last great urban waterfront redevelopment opportunities,” said Lewis George in a text message to The Washington Sun’s Martin Austermuhle.

The proposal for the 500,000-square-foot spa from Austrian wellness company Therme was an anchor for Mayor Muriel Bowser’s plans to redevelop Poplar Point, a 110-acre plot of riverfront land between the Frederick Douglass and 11th Street bridges.

Bowser’s pitch would give Therme 15 acres of the site for $1 in annual rent for 20 years, and the company said it would spend $500 million to build a new destination for the underserved side of the Anacostia River.

But the pitch fell flat with Lewis George, who has been more skeptical of D.C.’s historical tendency to give away public lands in exchange for development and benefits for residents. “This is prime waterfront real estate that should be used to leverage the building of more affordable homes and the creation of good jobs. The current proposal does neither. We must make this a better deal for District residents,” she told The Sun.

The clash between Bowser and Lewis George doesn’t just reflect the details of this deal, but also competing interests. Bowser is looking to cement her legacy with development deals, some that have been years in the making, while Lewis George is looking for opportunities to enact her own priorities once she takes office Jan. 2.

The news isn’t all bad for Bowser, though. Other development deals she has sent the council — including a proposal to build a new library and recreation center with housing on top in Chevy Chase — look to be moving forward.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Attorneys for D.C. Council member Trayon White, whose first bribery trial ended in a deadlocked jury and mistrial last month, are once again urging a federal judge to acquit him from the bench. “Trial revealed the Government’s undercover sting operation in this case to be a failure on many levels, worthy of the textbooks,” they wrote in a filing on Tuesday, arguing that while White accepted money from an FBI informant, he never intended to pressure government officials to extend the man’s city contracts.

White’s defense team is also arguing that the court should dismiss White’s case on double jeopardy grounds — though they acknowledged that doing so would be a “very unusual step.” Parties in the case are expected to meet at a hearing later this month to hash out these various legal arguments before the judge.

The D.C. Board of Elections has tossed out $16,000 in fines levied against Lewis George’s mayoral campaign ahead of the June primary, Martin reports. At the time the Office of Campaign Finance said Lewis George’s campaign impermissibly coordinated with local unions, but on Wednesday the elections board said there was no actual evidence of that.

D.C. Water says there has been no lasting harm to the Potomac River after a catastrophic sewage spill in January poured 243 million gallons of untreated waste into the water, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.

If you bought something to eat or drink at Capital One Arena last year, you could be entitled to a slice of a $4.5 million settlement over a 3% “venue fee” that Aramark vendors didn’t include on menu prices, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports. The settlement stemmed from a November 2025 lawsuit filed by the consumer advocacy group Travelers United that accused Aramark of “systematically cheating” customers and violating D.C. consumer protection laws.

Police say four teens have been charged in a string of eight home invasions around Northeast D.C., City Cast D.C. reports. The burglaries escalated over time, included stolen cars, and ended with an armed invasion and attempted sexual assault last week.

Marine One will now be required to give additional notification to air traffic control each time it takes off under a new policy implemented following a communication issue earlier this year which almost resulted in an in-air collision with a commercial jet, The Washington Post reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

A 911 call shows how staff at a Springfield group home mishandled the choking death of a nonverbal disabled resident in 2024, negligently claiming they were unable to help him by performing CPR, NBC4 reports.





FROM MARYLAND

Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin introduced a bill yesterday that calls on the Smithsonian to collect and display the massive banners depicting President Donald Trump that are draped over federal agencies as part of a "governmental propaganda" exhibit, Axios D.C. reports.





TALK TO TOM

Tom Sietsema is back and answering your questions about eating in the D.C. area. Submit your questions here.

How do you do this job without gaining a ton of weight? 

One of the first things I did when I became food critic of The Washington Post in 2000 was hire a trainer, which might sound like a yuppie affectation until you consider that the job involves constant eating out and no matter how careful you are, a steady stream of fried food, rich sauces, cocktails, meat, bread (gotta sample the bread baskets!) and desserts add up. I viewed exercise as insurance. Plus, you just feel better, mentally and physically, when you move more than your utensils from hand to mouth.

Here at The Sun, I’m still eating out as often as five or six meals a week. So at home, I eat pretty clean — fresh fruit and cottage cheese for breakfast is a near-daily habit. In restaurants, I rarely finish a dish, preferring to let others at the table do that or take home leftovers. (I hate wasting food, but I don’t necessarily want it in my fridge.) At this point, for instance, I can judge a steak in about three bites. And if it’s just two of us, I’ll order wine by the glass versus a bottle. Alice Waters of Chez Panisse fame once shared that her simple trick for losing weight was cutting out alcohol.

Restraint sounds boring, but that’s my mantra — unless, of course, I’m in front of a plate of french fries at Et Voila! in the Palisades or a tavern-style pizza at La Merna in Dupont Circle. “Moderation in moderation” is another rule I follow.

For more from Tom, check out this week’s Talk to Tom Q&A.





SPORTS

The Commanders are getting some reinforcements. Wednesday saw the return of several players from injury, with running backs Rachaad White and Jeremy McNichols, safety Nick Cross, cornerback Trey Amos, defensive lineman Deatrich Wise and right guard Sam Cosmi all practicing. For Wise, it was his first day back in over a year.

Quarterback Jayden Daniels, meanwhile, practiced for the first time in America since dislocating his left elbow, after getting in a few sessions last week in London — while sporting some extra protection on his arm.

"I was blessed enough to still be allowed to play this game," Daniels said after practice. "I'm going to embrace it. I'm going to embrace the brace."

entries.title: Morning Sun: The Pinch Hitters
entries.content:
Today’s notice: RFK Jr.’s star turn. Minnesota prepares to lose Medicaid funds. The Senate GOP walks away from North Carolina. Hinson v. Turek in Iowa. Schumer’s safe. And: Where the campaigns like to eat in D.C., with charts. 





THE LATEST

Who are the surrogates of 2026? Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been unmuzzled in recent months by a White House that used to try to keep him quiet, The Washington Sun’s Paige Winfield Cunningham and Christa Dutton report today. “They’ve given him flexibility to be himself and do his Bobby Kennedy thing,” a senior administration official said.

One reason: the midterms. RFK Jr.’s tirades against food additives and pesticides resonate with voters in both parties, our team writes. And: He’s slightly less disliked than other national GOP politicians.

“He represents a brand of politics and a constituency that is outside the normal coalition,” said Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Michigan), one of the battleground Republicans who has stumped with Kennedy.

Despite polls showing voters turned off by Donald Trump, the president keeps rallying for Republicans — and Republicans keep appearing with him. They’re fighting on turf Trump won in 2024, hoping the voters who backed him then still turn out for a midterm.

Speaker Mike Johnson and his leadership team are also doing big swings to Republican districts (mostly so they can stand up and call Democrats “communists”). Other big draws for Republicans on the stump: Vice President JD Vance and Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana).

On the other side of the aisle, Democrats find themselves in search of mainstream party figures. In Michigan, the party’s Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, has already campaigned with Kamala Harris and will appear soon with Barack Obama, despite the not-so-nice things he’s said about Obama’s presidency.

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) and former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel have been some of the most popular surrogates this cycle, a Democratic strategist familiar with House races told The Sun. All three are politicians who can cross the partisan divide and whom voters find relatable, the strategist said.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) has been doing some surrogate trips of his own. The Sun’s Jasmine Wright asked him, for fun, who the best surrogates would be if he could pick anyone, alive or dead. His picks were all dead: Martin Luther King Jr., Franklin D. Roosevelt and Frederick Douglass. With those guys unavailable, Mayor Pete, an astronaut and the guy who once put a dead fish in the mail will have to do.

More: Everything Is Bigger in Texas — Including the Number of Protests at Trump’s Rally • Forget ‘Kids’ — At the Trump Accounts Event, They’re ‘Shareholders’ • Election Deniers Have Trump’s Ear on a Voting Machine Conspiracy





FROM MINNESOTA


Scoop: White House’s Medicaid war is poised to escalate. Minnesota’s temporary human services commissioner, John Connolly, is preparing for federal health officials to officially withdraw up to $259 million in Medicaid payments the Trump administration froze earlier this year after reports of widespread fraud in state aid programs went viral. The Sun’s Natalie Alms and Paige Winfield Cunningham report on a fraud fight with Minnesota and California that could cost both states billions — even as the federal government has not offered specific evidence of fraud publicly or to state officials.

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


Republicans are officially on defense in red states: “You have conservative states with problems that can be fixed. Even in a bad environment, they’re solvable if you’re able to get the rural Republican base to show up. That’s pretty much where the cycle is at this point,” a Republican strategist told The Sun’s Al Weaver as Senate Republicans shift resources to Kansas and South Carolina.

Meanwhile, they’re all but giving up on North Carolina. The Raleigh News & Observer reported yesterday that GOP nominee Michael Whatley is pausing his ads so the campaign can rethink strategy. Al reports that the national party is pulling money out of the state to help shore things up in other places.

More: Turning Point USA Is Spending Millions to Boost One of the Last Candidates Endorsed by Charlie Kirk • Three More Political Committees Struck by Fraudsters

FROM IOWA


Ashley Hinson responds to Sun reporting from the debate stage: “My husband’s not a lobbyist, he’s an insurance agent,” the Republican nominee said during Iowa’s first Senate debate last night. “He works in our basement. He’s still working at home tonight while he’s home with our kids.”

The Sun reported in August that Hinson’s husband, Matt Arenholz, held a government affairs post at a leading insurance industry lobbying group and helped arrange meetings with Hinson and other members of the Iowa congressional delegation. At the debate last night, Democratic nominee Josh Turek briefly made an issue of the story, calling it “corruption that we have to address.”



FROM A POTENTIAL FUTURE


Chuck Schumer’s cruising altitude: With the Senate campaign map expanding for Democrats, the days when a vocal group was calling for a new leader in the Senate appear to be fading out of view, The Sun’s Igor Bobic reports. Schumer is planning to run for another term as leader in November, regardless of whether Democrats win the Senate or not. If they don’t, there appears to be little appetite in the caucus for anyone to actually try to challenge Schumer.

“Generally, this is a pretty conflict-averse group of people,” a Democratic senator told Igor.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Where the campaigns eat (and raise money): The Sun’s Stephen Neukam analyzed more than 1.6 million FEC reports and identified 829 restaurants in the D.C. area where campaigns have so far plunked down over $9 million in the 2026 cycle. The results: Republicans favor The Capital Grille, Joe’s Seafood, Ocean Prime, Trattoria Alberto and Bobby Van’s. Democrats prefer Paraiso, Osteria Morini, Ama, L’Ardente and Bistro Cacao.

Our food critic Tom Sietsema’s summary of the list: “convenience and proximity to power.”

What a GOP strategist said: “I just think Republicans like steak.”

entries.title: Minnesota Is Preparing for Trump to Cut Off Medicaid Payments
entries.summary: State officials say the Trump administration has indicated that it plans to pull hundreds of millions in federal dollars
entries.content:
The Trump administration has indicated to Minnesota that the state may soon be on the hook for hundreds of millions of dollars in Medicaid payments, Minnesota state officials told The Washington Sun.

The state is bracing for federal health officials to officially withdraw up to $259 million in Medicaid payments that the Trump administration froze earlier this year in the name of rooting out fraud, Minnesota’s temporary human services commissioner and state Medicaid director, John Connolly, said. The federal government deferred Medicaid payments to the state, pending review, after the administration alleged the state's Medicaid program raised red flags for fraud.

Federal officials have also suggested to the state that it could be required to cover even more Medicaid payments beyond the initial $259 million freeze, Connolly said, in what would be a major escalation of an already unprecedented course of action from the Trump administration.

Minnesota is one of two blue states caught in the administration’s crosshairs as it trumpets a war on Medicaid fraud ahead of the midterm elections. The other is California. The administration has made three quarterly deferrals of Medicaid reimbursements to Minnesota, totaling $550 million, and threatened to cut $2 billion from the state’s annual Medicaid funding through a separate process.

The federal government, however, has not offered specific evidence backing up its allegations of fraud to the states, California and Minnesota officials have told The Sun. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services declined to comment on its plans for Minnesota’s Medicaid dollars currently under review or on what information it has provided the state.

Connolly said Minnesota is ready to act on any “credible allegations of fraud.” But he said that “this feels increasingly like a war on Medicaid, not a war on fraud.”

“We are deeply concerned that this would be … another step in a retribution campaign for Minnesota that was promised very publicly,” he said.

The fraud task force’s focus on Minnesota and other blue states has played a central role in Republicans’ campaign messaging ahead of the midterms. CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, the former host of a wellness-focused TV show, has posted a constant stream of videos of himself going on fraud “stings” in U.S. cities. In its campaign, the Trump administration has touted misleading and unsubstantiated claims of fraud savings.

Vice President JD Vance, who is heading up the anti-fraud task force composed of officials from the Department of Health and Human Services, the Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission, announced over the summer that he was referring Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz — his former political opponent — and state Attorney General Keith Ellison to the DOJ for criminal fraud investigations.
Walz Vance AP-24276089886702 (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)Connolly wrote to Oz last week in a letter, reviewed by The Sun, asking for more details about how the federal agency has identified claims as suspicious.

“If there's information you have [or] methods you have you're not sharing, we're potentially paying fraudulent actors, criminals, really, in our program,” Connolly said of his inquiry. “We absolutely want to take prompt action if that's … happening in the program.”

State officials have been meeting with health providers to prepare them for the possibility of Washington officially taking back funding, Connolly said.

There is indisputably some amount of fraud in the Medicaid program, although the exact scope of the problem is difficult to calculate.

Minnesota has been under federal investigation for years for fraud in its safety-net programs, with some of it related to COVID-19 pandemic aid. The state has tagged certain Medicaid services as high-risk, freezing new providers and adding new reviews of claims. It has also revalidated thousands of providers as part of an anti-fraud effort stemming from the federal government’s threat to withhold up to $2 billion in funding. Before Trump’s second term, Ellison also led the state’s largest state Medicaid fraud prosecution.

A disallowance — the technical term for the denial of federal Medicaid matching funds to a state for expenditures that don’t meet federal requirements — can be related to fraud but is not necessarily always about fraud. Disallowances can also be tied to other problems with eligibility, benefits or administration, said Andy Schneider, who served as a senior adviser at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services during the Obama administration, where he focused on Medicaid program integrity

If the federal government does disallow funds, the state will have a chance to appeal the decision. Minnesota sued over the first deferment earlier this year, although a judge declined to issue a preliminary injunction. A stay is currently in place through early January.

States say the implications of these funding withdrawals could be serious. A permanent funding clawback would “force tough choices” for Minnesota given its structural budget deficit, Connolly said. He worries it could require the state to make difficult decisions “not only for the Medicaid program … but also roads, natural resources, public health.”

The Trump administration has also targeted $2.2 billion from California this year, alleging potential fraud in personal care services programs and other health programs — and putting those programs at risk for cuts in the process.

Minnesota, however, may face that uncertain future first.

“They have done to Minnesota what CMS has never done to any other state,” Schneider said of the scale of the administration’s actions against the state. “It’s all uncharted territory.”

entries.title: D.C. Elections Board Tosses Out Fines Against Janeese Lewis George
entries.summary: Lewis George’s campaign was accused of illegally coordinating with local unions.
entries.content:
The D.C. Board of Elections on Wednesday tossed out $16,000 in fines that had been levied against Janeese Lewis George’s mayoral campaign, rejecting claims from campaign finance regulators that she had impermissibly coordinated with local unions ahead of the June primary she ended up winning. 

The ruling is a long-awaited win for Lewis George, albeit one that now seems relatively inconsequential. Despite the rancor that the original investigation by the D.C. Office of Campaign Finance stirred up only days before the primary, she handily defeated challenger Kenyan McDuffie and is expected to win the November general election.

The initial OCF investigation claimed that the close relationship between Lewis George’s campaign and local unions — so close that union staff took leave from their jobs to work on her campaign — amounted to illegal coordination, notably because it allegedly involved a union-backed committee that raised more than $1.5 million to run ads supporting her candidacy.

But her campaign argued that there was no actual evidence that it illicitly coordinated with unions and that a firewall existed between campaign staff and their union jobs. After hours of discussion on Wednesday, the board’s three members unanimously agreed.

“You have no evidence to show there was impropriety,” said board Chair Greg McCarthy to officials with OCF, which regulates and investigates campaign spending during local elections.

In a statement, Lewis George said she welcomed the board’s ruling and said the investigation wasn’t handled properly.

“OCF’s order violated D.C. procedural requirements, included multiple false statements about its own investigation, misrepresented the campaign’s statements and positions, offered no evidence in support of their conclusions, and was simply wrong on the law,” she said. “And it was not the first time OCF had filed a flawed order in the days just before a contested election.”

Lewis George was referring to a similar incident in 2022, when OCF declared only days before an election that At-Large D.C. Council member Elissa Silverman had misspent public campaign funds on a poll. Silverman ended up losing that election to McDuffie, and months later the Board of Elections tossed out the OCF findings against Silverman.

That history seemed to work its way into Wednesday’s hearing, when McCarthy pressed OCF attorney William SanFord on why he unveiled the investigation and fines late on a Friday only four days before the primary.

“We had no motivation to try and influence the election and issue an order to embarrass a candidate in that cycle,” SanFord said.

“It just happened to be four days before the election?” McCarthy said.

“That was not a consideration,” SanFord replied.

In a statement, Ward 1 council member Brianne Nadeau welcomed the board’s decision, while reiterating that she had asked the D.C. Inspector General to look into the way OCF handled the investigation into Lewis George’s campaign.

“I'm glad that the Board of Elections reviewed the information before them and concluded that there was no evidence of any wrongdoing by the Janeese Lewis George campaign. My request of the Inspector General was to determine how it came about that findings rooted in no evidence came to be issued in the 11th hour of a campaign this time and during prior campaigns. I believe my request remains relevant,” she said.

Lewis George added her own criticism of OCF. “D.C. voters deserve a fair election process that inspires confidence and where all rules are consistently and fairly enforced,” she said.
