entries.title: Teixeira Is Making a Play for a Seat on the House Financial Services Panel
entries.summary: The former professional baseball player is leaning into his ties to Wall Street and Texas firms.
entries.content:
Mark Teixeira, who is poised to win a House seat in Texas, is vying for a seat on the powerful House Financial Services Committee — leaning on his ties as an ex-Yankee and Texan.

His bid for the prime panel slot comes as Texas tries to rival New York as the country’s economic hub. Large financial institutions have either relocated or expanded their operational departments to the state. Texas’ comparatively inexpensive real estate and business-friendly regulations are big draws for companies as they lure employees.

To help his party in the midterms, Teixeira, 46, has crisscrossed the country with leadership, visiting swing districts in New York and New Jersey to campaign for Republican incumbents in tight races.

In August, he joined Speaker Mike Johnson to stump for Rep. Tom Kean Jr. in New Jersey at the Hawk Pointe Golf Club for a breakfast fundraiser. That same month, he wolfed down pizza with the speaker and Rep. Mike Lawler at Silvio’s Pizzeria in Thornwood, New York. This week, Teixeira helped lead a trip with Republican Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota — and nearly a dozen Texas candidates — at the U.S.-Mexico border.

“He’s doing all the right things,” said a Republican House member who sits on the Financial Services panel. “He is raising money for others, campaigning for others and he has a great financial background.”

Teixeira, who is running in Texas’ 21st Congressional District, told The Washington Sun he raised his hand to pitch in. “I have a very unique profile, obviously, with my baseball career, and I want to use that to help the team. It's really that simple.”

He said after he won his primary in March, he reached out to the House GOP campaign arm and said: “‘Hey, listen, my number one priority is in my district and to spend as much time as possible talking with voters, talking with constituents. But in my free time, I'm willing to go travel and help out anybody that is going to be in a tight race.’”

Teixeira already has support for a committee slot from Rep. Pete Sessions, the incoming dean of the Texas delegation, who also serves on the panel. Teixeira also confirmed his interest in Financial Services in an interview with The Sun this week.

Sessions told The Sun about his likely future colleague, “I would just call it a well-heeled district that comes out of Austin, Texas, which is a very important economic driver for the state of Texas.” He added, “I had a direct conversation with him about how I felt like that would be a match for him — he and his district.”

Sessions said he personally introduced Teixeira to members of the committee and that the former major leaguer also has the support of Rep. Roger Williams, another senior Texan, and the rest of the delegation. “French Hill is very excited about it,” Sessions said of the current Financial Services chair.

As a baseball player, Teixeira spent significant time in Texas (where he started his 13-year career) and New York (where he ended it). A power-hitting first baseman, Teixeira debuted with the Rangers in 2003, then joined the Yankees in 2009, where he was named an All-Star that summer before helping them win the World Series that fall. For a stretch, he was one of the biggest names in the sport. And now, as he launches his political career in Texas, he counts Jamie Dimon, CEO of JPMorgan Chase, and David Solomon, CEO of Goldman Sachs, as friends, according to one lobbyist.

But even with that background and Republican colleagues pushing him for Financial Services, Teixeira’s chances could hinge, at least in part, on how many seats Republicans have after the November midterm elections.

“We have at least six openings. There are at least four sophomores or freshmen in waiting,” a Republican member on the committee told The Sun. “It isn’t out of the realm of the possibility, and if he promises to play baseball his chances improve,” referring to the GOP’s Congressional Baseball team.

Teixeira said he realizes he’s different from other incoming freshmen and that is why he’s made it a point to help his future classmates.

“Whether that's because of a Yankees connection, a Braves connection, a Rangers connection, whatever it might be, you know, I have that national profile to be able to bring people that otherwise may not support Republican candidates, but are interested in Mark Teixeira coming to the district,” he said.

Financial Services is a prime committee but has not been a barrier for freshmen members. Throughout the last two cycles, Republicans have placed several new members on the committee, including Lawler and Reps. Monica De La Cruz of Texas and Mike Haridopolos of Florida.

Leadership will determine the number of committee slots between the two parties at the start of next Congress. The committee currently has 30 Republican seats versus 23 seats for Democrats. The prospect of Republicans losing seats could complicate Teixeira’s bid, but he comes in with quite the resume — especially as sports and politics are mixing as much as ever.

“I don't want to be transactional, where the only time I'm talking with my colleagues is when I need something from them or I need them to support a bill that's good for my district,” Teixeira said. “I want to have great relationships with all of my colleagues. What that turns into, we'll see.”

Teixeira is not the only ex-athlete vying for a House seat this cycle. Former Jets kicker Jay Feely is running in Arizona, where his opponent, Democrat Amish Shah, was actually the Jets’ team doctor while Feely was on the team.

President Donald Trump made sports a key part of the America250 celebration this summer, including the UFC fight on the White House lawn, the Grand Prix on the National Mall and the Patriot Games. There was also political posturing around the World Cup, which the U.S. hosted along with Mexico and Canada. And on the Hill, the Senate recently passed a college sports bill that now faces an uncertain path in the House.

Some key debates impacting sports will continue after the midterms and into the next Congress. Once the MLB playoffs finish later this month the league is expected to deal with a major labor battle. With the current collective bargaining agreement expiring on Dec. 1, the expectation is that the owners will lock the players out amid long-simmering tension. A key part of negotiations will be whether the next CBA includes a salary cap, which the owners favor and the players do not.

It is unclear how or whether Washington will get involved in negotiations between the team owners and the Major League Baseball Players Association. Teixeira, though, could be an interesting figure on that front. In 2020, as the players and owners were at odds over money during the pandemic, Teixeira appeared on ESPN to urge the players to accept the deal in front of them. He said that he would usually encourage players to hold out for better terms. But in that case, he reasoned that playing hard ball, so to speak, could lose fans that might never come back.

That interview was well before he jumped into Republican politics — and, of course, before he was interested in joining the Financial Services committee. Trump has already endorsed MLB adding a salary cap in the next CBA, siding with the owners. In an uncapped system, Teixeira made more than $200 million in his career, including the eight-year, $180 million contract he signed with the Yankees in 2009. That was also the last time the team won the World Series.

And while that all adds to the buzz around Teixeira as an incoming member, future Republican colleagues may be even more interested in whether he’ll suit up for the Congressional Baseball Game next summer.

“You got to know, we think this is like drafting the first-round pick for the baseball team,” Sessions said. “He’s already signed. We’ve inked that deal. NIL, fortunately, was not a part of it.”

entries.title: Army Finds Systemic Failures Behind D.C. Midair Collision
entries.summary: The report identified failures involving air traffic control, helicopter routes, training and safety practices.
entries.content:
By Josh Funk

The U.S. Army found systemic safety breakdowns behind last year’s midair collision between an American Airlines jet and a Black Hawk helicopter near Washington, D.C., and recommended changes to prevent future tragedies.

The Army report — completed in May and released publicly Thursday after months of pressure from the victims' families — identified failures involving air traffic control, helicopter routes, training and safety practices. The Associated Press obtained a copy of the report hours before it was released.

The deadliest plane crash on U.S. soil in over two decades happened when the helicopter collided with the descending airliner as it approached the runway, sending both plummeting into the icy Potomac River and killing 67.

The Army report highlighted how the air traffic controller at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport could have prevented the crash, but it also acknowledged the military’s own failings and other contributing factors.

Tim Lilley, a former Army Black Hawk pilot whose son Sam Lilley was the airliner's first officer, said the report leaves important questions unanswered. Parts were redacted, and responsibility for the Army's failures was assigned broadly rather than to individuals.

“The Army owes the families and the American public a full accounting of how these risks were allowed to persist, who was responsible for the decisions that allowed them to persist and what will be done to make sure this never happens again,” said Lilley, now a commercial jet captain.

The Army acknowledged that in a statement Thursday.

“We recognize the families’ need for answers and remain committed to transparency regarding the Army’s review,” it said.

While the report largely reinforces the National Transportation Safety Board's conclusions, the civilian investigation was broader and emphasized years of missed warnings by the Federal Aviation Administration along with a weak military safety culture.

The Army faulted the air traffic controller for not giving the helicopter crew more precise information about the approaching jet and for not warning the jet’s pilot about the helicopter. After the crash, the FAA prohibited controllers from relying on pilots to maintain visual separation in busy airspace.

The report recommended looking beyond Washington to examine military helicopter operations in other major cities for similar risks. An Army official said the review of helicopter flights in other cities, including Los Angeles and the Seattle-Tacoma region, is ongoing. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the situation publicly.

The lieutenant general who authored the report cited “breakdowns across all layers of conflict management” but singled out two failed radio transmissions that contributed to the helicopter crew not identifying the jet. The military pilots' night-vision goggles also restricted their view and made it hard to spot the plane amid the city lights.

The poorly designed helicopter route allowed a scant 75 feet (23 meters) of vertical separation between a helicopter and a plane landing on the airport's secondary runway, assuming helicopters stayed near the riverbank, which the route didn't require. This did not allow enough separation to account for the accepted level of error in a Black Hawk’s altimeter, and the NTSB found the helicopter was flying nearly 100 feet (30 meters) higher than its instruments read.

The NTSB said in a letter to the Army last week that it was pleased with the Army's progress on seven of its eight safety recommendations. That contrasts with the FAA’s failure to implement roughly a third of the recommendations aimed at the agency.

The Army said it has strengthened helicopter crew training, and has inspected and reconfigured 3,585 helicopters after discovering the crashed Black Hawk's ADS-B Out system, which broadcasts its location, hadn't been working for some time.

The military is also improving its monitoring of safety risks and working with the FAA to share information about close calls.

Families of the crash victims said the Army's findings strengthen their case for legislation requiring aircraft to have technology that helps pilots detect nearby traffic.

“It’s a simple concept anyone can understand: aircraft should be able to see each other in the sky. The technology is proven. All that’s required is the political will to do the right thing,” the Families of Flight 5342 group said in a statement Thursday.

“We have waited long enough. We waited for the NTSB. We waited for the Army. Both investigations are complete, and both make clear that collision avoidance technology must be part of the solution. There is nothing left for Congress to wait for,” they said.

The House and Senate have passed separate aviation safety bills but have yet to agree on a final version.

Associated Press writer Konstantin Toropin in Washington contributed.

entries.title: Mary Peltola Was Pressed on Transgender Rights at a Campaign Event
entries.summary: The Alaska Democrat told the protester that she hopes “we don’t have to spend one second on a conversation about trans anything” if she gets to the Senate.
entries.content:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska — A protester confronted Senate Democratic nominee Mary Peltola during a Thursday campaign event over a recent TV ad that critics viewed as anti-trans, pressing the former congresswoman to pledge that she would stand up for transgender rights if elected to Congress this year.

The person confronting Peltola, 23-year-old Nico Wilkerson, later told The Washington Sun that he was no longer planning to vote for the former congresswoman because of her views on trans issues, underscoring the broader difficulty Democratic candidates face this election season as they try to navigate a relentless series of Republican attacks.

Peltola had arrived at a senior center in Anchorage to campaign a few weeks before facing Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in one of the year’s most competitive Senate races. She took a wide range of questions from the audience, which mostly comprised senior citizens, before Wilkerson was handed a microphone.

He asked Peltola about a recent ad in which the candidate, in a response to Republican attacks, said she doesn’t “want kids getting surgeries to change genders, or men in girls’ bathrooms.”

“That is a Republican slander,” Wilkerson told Peltola on Thursday. ”That is a false slander, and you are buying into it by releasing that ad. So my question for you is, do you plan to support trans rights in the Senate if you are elected?”

Peltola did not answer the question directly, saying that the GOP attacks on trans issues were “political theater” meant to distract from the high cost of energy and food.

“My hope is that we don’t have to spend one second on a conversation about trans anything,” she said. “My hope is that we have a Senate that’s serious about fixing American problems and not creating political diversions, not creating and stoking wedge issues that just divide us.”

Democrats this election are more forcefully pushing back on GOP attacks related to trans issues, convinced that their lack of an aggressive response during the 2024 presidential election cost the party votes. The party’s messaging this time around has generally been similar to Peltola’s, with many candidates saying that they don’t believe trans children should be allowed to participate in girls’ sports or reiterating their opposition to gender reassignment surgery for minors.

Democrats have worked hard behind the scenes over the last two years to craft a response to the attacks that satisfies moderates but doesn’t alienate trans people or allies. Some party strategists have said that liberal groups focused on the issue, like the American Civil Liberties Union, have seemingly given the candidates more space this election to respond to GOP attacks without garnering extensive criticism from progressive institutions.

But Wilkerson's frustration shows the extent to which Democratic candidates can still face backlash on the issue from individual voters.

In an interview with The Sun after the event, Wilkerson, who is a transgender man, said he had spoken with Peltola about trans issues weeks earlier at another campaign event in town. At the time, he asked the former representative about a vote she took while in Congress that would deny military families coverage if their child tried to receive gender-affirming care.

“And she said, ‘I wanted to get elected,’” Wilkerson said. “That's what she said: ‘I wanted to get elected.’”

Peltola ended that conversation by telling Wilkerson that Republicans’ attacks against transgender people were unfair.

But a week later, Wilkerson said he saw Peltola’s ad, which he believed reaffirmed the worst GOP talking points about the transgender community instead of rebutting them. And so he decided to confront her Thursday.

“This was my only chance to speak to her directly and let her know the impact of her ad,” Wilkerson told The Sun. “Let her know that I felt personally betrayed by her ad, let her know that she is playing into Republican lies and slander against trans people.”

entries.title: Pentagon Says Fort Hood Shooter's Execution Will Be Livestreamed
entries.summary: Nidal Malik Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009.
entries.content:
By Konstantin Toropin

The Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be “public.”

Hegseth, speaking to the conservative TV outlet Real America’s Voice News on Wednesday, said the execution of Hasan will take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3. Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public,” Hegseth said.

Hegseth spoke to the outlet aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier while visiting the long-deployed crew, who supported the Iran war, before their arrival at their home port in San Diego.

When asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration, Hegseth simply replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3rd.”

Officials in the Pentagon clarified Thursday that the execution will be livestreamed and that more details would follow.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said Monday that President Donald Trump had approved the execution of Hasan.

Trump has previously been critical of public executions in Iran, at times using the possibility of protesters being killed by the Iranian government as a possible rationale for military action. Those warnings preceded his ultimate choice to attack Iran at the end of February over its ballistic missiles and the risk of it developing nuclear weapons.

“We’ve been told that the killing in Iran is stopping,” Trump told reporters on Jan. 14 of this year. “It’s stopping and there’s no plan for executions.”

He repeated that claim on Jan. 20 at a White House press briefing, saying: “We let them know that if that happens, that will be a very bad day for them. And they decided not to do it. They didn’t hang the people.”

Slightly more than a month later in his State of the Union address, Trump said, “We stopped them from hanging a lot of them with the threat of serious violence.”

The White House on Thursday immediately referred questions about the plans for the livestreamed execution to the Pentagon.

However, experts on military law said Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution.

“It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions,” Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law.

Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building where soldiers were were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun.

During the trial it was revealed that Hasan spent weeks planning the deadly attack, and his preparation included videotaping a sales clerk showing him how to change the magazine on the pistol that he purchased. He would later go to a gun range outside Austin and ask for advice on how to reload with speed and precision from an instructor.

Soldiers later testified that Hasan’s rapid reloading made it all but impossible to stop the shooting. Investigators recovered 146 shell casings inside the building and dozens more outside, where Hasan shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.

Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defense during his trial. Hasan made almost no effort to defend himself in court, telling jurors when he acted as his own counsel that evidence would show he was the shooter and describing himself as a soldier who had “switched sides.”

Hegseth said the military hasn’t executed a servicemember by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.

entries.title: Maduro Faces New Charge of Torture of Venezuelans and Americans
entries.summary: An updated indictment details the experiences of nine unnamed victims who were arrested related to efforts to quell protests or other political issues.
entries.content:
The government has accused former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife of personally approving the torture of political prisoners — including Americans — as part of a conspiracy to punish political opposition, silence dissent and preserve their political power.

An updated indictment unsealed Thursday with a charge of conspiracy to commit torture sharply raises the stakes in the ongoing prosecution in Manhattan federal court of Maduro, who already faced multiple offenses including conspiracy to commit narco-terrorism and conspiracy to import cocaine.

Prosecutors, over 10 of the indictment’s 30 pages, described how Maduro employed his vast network of resources — including the feared General Directorate of Military Counterintelligence, the DGCIM, and the leftist narco paramilitary Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, the FARC.

Prosecutors say his jailed co-defendant and wife, Cilia Adela Flores de Maduro, a former high-ranking government official, also took part, once approving the kidnapping and torture of a half dozen soldiers in an attempt to root out dissention among the military ranks.

The indictment details the experiences of nine unnamed victims who were arrested in relation to efforts to quell protests or other political issues and then beaten, given electric shocks, deprived of food and water. It describes how Maduro would “decide, on a case-by-case basis, whether an individual who had been abused would be released or subjected to criminal prosecution.”

If they refused to talk, he “would ask questions including, ‘What can we do to make them talk?’” — sometimes making “suggestions for particular torture techniques, saying ‘do not let them sleep,’ or ‘pour water on them,’ at times laughing after hearing about the abuse of prisoners,” the indictment says.

The indictment describes the experiences of one American prisoner who was taken to Boleíta Norte prison, where he was given electroshocks and guards injected him with a mysterious substance that gave him seizures — all while accusing him of being part of a grand American conspiracy to kill Maduro.

The indictment also tells the story of another unidentified American who was visiting his family in August 2023 when he was allegedly kidnapped by DGCIM, beaten so hard from behind that he required hospital treatment, and at one point had a pistol shoved into his mouth and told to “say goodbye to everyone he knew.”

Guards at Boleíta Norte prison later electrocuted his testicles — and told him the only reason he remained alive was for a future prisoner swap with the United States, the indictment says.

Many of the torture scenes described in the superseding indictment relate to Maduro’s desperate attempts to maintain political control in Venezuela during the years when his regime struggled to remain in power. That includes a 2017 constitutional crisis when the Maduro loyalists in the nation’s supreme court took over the country’s legislature and 2024 sham presidential election that was widely censured around the globe.

But it also describes the depths of the suffering experienced by the Venezuelan people, thousands of whom have fled to neighboring countries and the United States.

Prosecutors in one segment of the indictment describe what played out behind the scenes as Maduro’s regime tried to hunt down a law enforcement officer who “had become a famous opponent of the regime,” since he one time flew a stolen helicopter around Caracas and another time stole weapons from a military command station.

That matches the actions of Óscar Alberto Pérez, a state police investigator who briefly became a hero when he went rogue in 2017 by stealing a helicopter, dropping nonlethal stun grenades on the Supreme Tribunal of Justice building, and documented his acts of resistance on social media.

Prosecutors say in the indictment that one of the law enforcement officer’s friends was arrested on January 4, 2018, by government security forces in a futile attempt to locate the renegade cop. A high-ranking Venezuelan official was physically present when the man was tortured for days and had his testicles electrocuted while interrogators threatened to kill his child, the indictment says.

In another instance, prosecutors in the indictment say Maduro personally ordered the kidnapping and torture of a Venezuelan military officer who was under suspicion of meeting with a former Venezuelan government official who’d joined the political opposition.

The man was tortured by the DGCIM: forced to experience simulated drowning 30 times, beaten and subjected to live wire electrocutions 20 times — only to experience further torture when he was taken to a FARC camp in rural neighboring Colombia. Maduro allegedly viewed a video recording of the man’s forced false confession, the indictment says.

Prosecutors also alleged that in 2022 Maduro summoned several judges to his presidential palace to bribe them with a $1,000 monthly stipend to issue rulings favorable to his administration. But when one judge refused secret orders to yank opposition political opponents from appearing on electoral ballots, her family members were “arrested and tortured” by the DGCIM, the indictment says.

The indictment details how one family member was forced to drink latrine water, subjected to tear gas in their jail cell and subjected to extreme conditions inside a freezing room with blaring noise where bright lights were kept on at all times — until the judge finally relented.

Maduro and his wife, who were taken from their official home in Venezuela on Jan. 3, 2026, during an American military operation, previously pleaded not guilty of the narcotics charges and have questioned the U.S. government’s legal ability to abduct and criminally charge a foreign head of state.

entries.title: Days After Woman Found Dead Near a U.S. Base in Japan, Alcohol Will Be Allowed Again
entries.summary: Active-duty personnel were barred from alcohol in the wake of the death, but troops will be allowed to imbibe during a “period of reflection.”
entries.content:
U.S. troops in Okinawa, Japan, will be permitted to drink alcohol during the U.S. military’s upcoming 30-day “period of reflection,” a move that follows a ban on active-duty imbibing in the wake of the death of a Japanese woman authorities allege was strangled by a U.S. Marine.

Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, was arrested Sunday in connection with the death of Anna Yagi, 39. Authorities there say Ballard strangled Yagi in a Naha hotel room Saturday and stole her personal items, The Associated Press reported.

Ballard had been based at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma at the time of the alleged crimes, according to local outlets. He’s denied the allegations.

Earlier this week, the U.S. military instituted a 48-hour alcohol ban for all active-duty personnel as part of a “period of rraining,” as the military put it, which began on Wednesday and will run through Friday. The ban applies to private residences but not to civilian employees, contractors, family members or dependents.

A III Marine Expeditionary Force spokesperson, 1st Lt. Tyler Thomas, confirmed the drinking development to Stars and Stripes on Thursday.

“Standard off-duty regulations and responsible-use policies will remain in effect outside of curfew hours,” he said.

The training period includes an operational pause and mandatory discussions on off-duty behavior, enforcement mechanisms, alcohol awareness, Okinawan culture and alliance responsibilities, according to a memo written by Lt. Gen. Benjamin T. Watson, the Okinawa area coordinator and commanding general of III Marine Expeditionary Force.

Following the training period, a 30-day “period of reflection” will commence. It was previously unknown whether soldiers would be allowed to drink during that time.

During the monthlong stretch, troops must adhere to a curfew from midnight to 5 a.m. Watson said the restrictions are to remind soldiers that “liberty is a privilege and a collective responsibility.”

The U.S. military will also undertake a review of off-duty behavior, policies and procedures as part of the reflection period. Officials will provide recommendations to the Okinawa Area Coordinating Committee for potential implementation.

In an FAQ page, the U.S. military said it is implementing force-wide measures because “incidents of this nature demand a pause for reflection. Every interaction with the people of Okinawa either builds or undermines the trust essential to our alliance.”

The U.S. military has had a presence in Okinawa since 1945. About 70% of the nation’s military presence in Japan is in the region. A bilateral agreement allows more than 50,000 American troops to be based in Japan.

However, the recent death has raised concerns regarding relations between the two countries.

In a meeting between Genta Koja, the governor of the Okinawa prefecture, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Koja asked the Japanese government to reduce the burden of hosting U.S. troops on the island, the AP reported.

According to the Okinawan newspaper Ryukyu Shimpo, between 1972 and 2023, 6,124 U.S. military members were arrested for criminal offenses — 759 of those for crimes such as murder, robbery and sexual assault, according to a 2024 police report obtained by the outlet.

“Okinawa has requested preventive measures every time similar crimes were repeated in past, and now we have this case again,” Koja told Takaichi in front of reporters.

entries.title: Afternoon Sun: Fit Happens
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Afternoon Sun newsletter for Oct. 8, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Scoop: The White House is floating Russ Vought’s deputy, Eric Ueland, to lead the Government Accountability Office. The OMB deputy director has presided over massive federal workforce shakeups that Congress’ watchdog arm has deemed detrimental.

Cut him some slacks? Donald Trump’s former tailor spoke with The Washington Sun’s Jenna Monnin about the online frenzy stirred up by the president’s Jos. A. Bank suit — a budget-friendly change of pace for the man who usually gets luxury tailoring.





THE ADMINISTRATION

Trump made 517 personal trades of stocks, bonds or other financial funds in August, including purchases between $1 million and $5 million each in Microsoft, McDonald’s and Comcast stock.

The administration is blocking Microsoft and Adobe from giving foreign workers temporarily living and working in the U.S. a pathway to permanent residency, accusing the companies of fraud.

Democrats are calling for the firing of Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, after a bombshell report that she sought $100,000 from a Trump donor while offering access to administration officials.

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and her daughter have separately met with senior figures from Bosnia’s pro-Russian Serb nationalist leadership in recent weeks, photos circulating online this week show.





THE HILL

Mike Johnson floated a potential pivot after the midterms: “If we lose this majority or whatever, I don’t know what my next chapter of life is,” the House speaker told Fox News’ Aishah Hasnie today. “If God moves on our hearts and says we should, you know, go back to my hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business, I'll do that with equal fervor.”

  • “We’re going to need every dollar” of the estimated $450 million raised by the party last quarter, Johnson told reporters while stumping for House candidate Derek Merrin in Ohio. “It’s an all-time record, but it’s an expensive cycle.”
Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut) told reporters he confronted Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Qatar’s emir during a Middle East trip this week over Trump’s “corruption of foreign policy,” including Saudi investments in Jared Kushner’s private equity fund and Qatar’s gift of a luxury jet.

  • Murphy said both leaders defended their dealings as legitimate business, The Sun’s Joe Gould reports. But the senator warned bin Salman that a Democratic takeover of Congress after the midterms could bring “serious investigations.”
Saving College Sports, a pro-Protect College Sports Act group led by Cody Campbell, sent a memo warning that four ACC schools — including Florida State University and the University of Miami — are organizing to tank the bill’s chances in the House over a conference cap provision.





THE CAMPAIGN TRAILRepublican Mark Teixeira, who is poised to win a House seat in Texas, is vying for a seat on the powerful House Financial Services Committee — leaning on his ties as an ex-Yankee and Texan.

Pennsylvania Democrat Janelle Stelson says DHS wrongly accused her campaign of employing an undocumented immigrant who was arrested for indecent exposure and disorderly conduct.

Senate Leadership Fund is shifting $1.85 million initially allocated for broadcast ads in Georgia to South Carolina, per AdImpact. John Thune’s super PAC already shifted $5 million to Sen. Darline Graham earlier this week.

  • Two new Texas Senate digital media buys just dropped: An affiliate of Chuck Schumer’s super PAC disclosed $3.7 million, while an SLF affiliate disclosed $5.1 million.




THE COURTS

A U.S. district judge temporarily extended White House access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico following a hearing today on Trump’s media ban. The Sun has signed ontoan amicus brief filed in this case in support of the news outlets.

The Supreme Court once again quickly stepped into a legal clash regarding the rules governing the price of political television ads ahead of the midterms.

The NFL wants state regulators, not the federal government, to oversee and regulate prediction markets such as Kalshi, the league wrote in a Supreme Court filing today.
